Here are the verse-by-verse notes on Hebrews 13, drawn from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Hebrews 13 – Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — "Continue in brotherly love."

The Greek word here is *philadelphia*, meaning brotherly friendship and affection — the love of deep friendship and partnership (rather than *agape*, the self-giving love, or *eros*, erotic love). The writer assumes this love already exists among believers and simply urges that it "continue." Ellicott notes that their love for the Christian brotherhood had been commended earlier (Heb 6:10), yet there was ground for fear that such affection might not continue (Heb 10:25). Gill adds that "continue" means not the internal grace itself (which, once present, never departs) but the exercise and increase of it — abounding in it more and more.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 2 — "Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it."

Hospitality to Christian brethren traveling from distant homes is especially intended (Ellicott). In the ancient world, inns were notorious for immorality, so Christians needed to open their homes to fellow believers (Guzik). The Greek word for hospitality (*philoxenia*) literally means "love for strangers" — brotherly love extended to all believers, not just friends. The reference to entertaining angels recalls Abraham (Gen 18) and Lot (Gen 19). Clement of Rome (c. AD 95) appealed to these same examples: "For his faith and hospitality a son was given to Abraham in his old age. For his hospitality and godliness Lot was saved from Sodom" (Ellicott). Guzik also cites the *Didache* (c. AD 90–110), which set rules to prevent abuse of Christian hospitality by false prophets: anyone staying more than two days or asking for money was a false prophet.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 3 — "Remember those in prison as if you were bound with them, and those who are mistreated as if you were suffering with them."

This refers first to those imprisoned for the Gospel (Guzik, Gill). The phrase "as bound with them" means by true fellow-feeling making oneself a sharer in their lot — or, alternatively, mindful that all Christians are Christ's prisoners in service (Ellicott). "As being yourselves also in the body" means remembering that we too dwell in a body liable to pain and may suffer ill-treatment for Christ (Ellicott). Gill adds that this applies also to those suffering spiritual adversity, such as prevailing corruption, the hidings of God's face, or Satan's temptations.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 4 — "Marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers."

Ellicott reads this as an exhortation: "Let marriage be held in honour among all, and let the bed be undefiled." It is directed against both impurity (cf. Heb 12:16) and false asceticism that forbade marriage (1 Tim 4:3). The lax morals of Gentiles and prevalence of divorce among Jews explain the sharp warning. Guzik notes that the Bible celebrates sex within marriage (as in the Song of Solomon) but condemns sex outside it. "Fornicators" refers to those who have sex without the marriage commitment; "adulterers" to those unfaithful to marriage vows. Bruce (quoted by Guzik) clarifies: "Fornication and adultery are not synonymous in the New Testament: adultery implies unfaithfulness by either party to the marriage vow, while the word translated 'fornication' covers a wide range of sexual irregularities."

**Denominational note — Catholic vs. Protestant on celibacy:** Gill, a Baptist, explicitly condemns "the Papists, who deny it [marriage] to men employed in sacred work" as violating the statement that marriage is honourable "in all." This reflects the historic Protestant objection to mandatory clerical celibacy. The Catholic tradition, by contrast, has read this verse as affirming the goodness of marriage for the laity while upholding consecrated celibacy as a higher calling (1 Cor 7:32–34). The Council of Trent anathematized anyone who said "that the marriage state is to be placed above the state of virginity, or of celibacy" (Session XXIV, Canon X).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 5 — "Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: 'Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.'"

Ellicott notes the connection between vv. 4–5: impurity and covetousness "may be said to divide between them nearly the whole domain of human selfishness and vice" (Lightfoot, cited by Ellicott). The promise is a composite from Deuteronomy 31:6, Genesis 28:15, Joshua 1:5, and 1 Chronicles 28:20 — not an exact quotation but clearly drawn from these texts (Ellicott). Spurgeon, cited by Guzik, observes that the Greek has five negatives: "I will not, not leave thee; I will never, no never, forsake thee." Guzik notes that contentment is rooted in God's promise, not in possessions — contentment "has much more to do with what you are on the inside rather than what you have." Spurgeon preached: "There is no room to be covetous, no excuse for being covetous, for God hath said, 'I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.'"

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/hebrews/hebrews-13.cfm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_135-7

### v. 6 — "So we say with confidence: 'The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can man do to me?'"

This quotes Psalm 118:6. Ellicott renders it: "so that we say with courage." The confidence is the direct result of the promise in v. 5 — if God will never leave us, we need not fear anything man can do. Guzik observes: "Strangely we are often more likely to put security and find contentment in things that are far less reliable and secure than God Himself is." Gill notes that the ground of fearlessness is "the infinite power, grace, and goodness of God" and that the utmost man can do is "kill the body."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 7 — "Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith."

Ellicott translates "which have the rule" as "which were your leaders" — past tense, indicating these spiritual guides had been removed by death. "Considering the outcome of their conduct" means contemplating the blessed end of their Christian life and course, which strengthens others to imitate their faith (Ellicott). Guzik adds: leaders don't need to be perfect, but they should demonstrate by their life that the power of Jesus is real and transformative — "that demonstrates a faith that can actually be followed." Gill notes that "faith" here can mean their faithfulness in duty, the grace of faith they exercised, the profession of faith they held, or the doctrine of faith they taught.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 8 — "Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever."

This stands as an independent declaration, not grammatically dependent on v. 7. Ellicott explains: "Their earlier guides have passed away; their Lord and Saviour abides the same for ever." "Yesterday" reaches back to the lifetime of the departed teachers; "today" is the present; "forever" reaches into eternity. Albert Barnes (via CCEL) emphasizes this as an "irrefragable proof of the divinity of the Saviour. It asserts immutability — sameness in the past, the present, and to all eternity — but of whom can this be affirmed but God?" Gill notes that "the same" (*ho autos*) answers to the Hebrew *Hu*, a name of God in Psalm 102:27, expressive of "eternity, immutability, and independence." The unchanging nature of Jesus provides the measure for all Christian conduct — we should not expect something completely "new" from a "new Jesus" (Guzik).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/13.htm
- https://ccel.org/ccel/barnes/ntnotes/ntnotes.xxii.xiii.viii.html

### v. 9 — "Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace and not by foods of no value to those devoted to them."

Ellicott notes the better Greek reading: "Be not carried away by divers and strange teachings." The "teachings" were various and foreign to the one true word. The contrast between "grace" and "meats" reveals the nature of the error: doctrines and practices similar to those Paul censured in Colossians 2:16–23 — human additions to Mosaic law and perversions of its spirit (Ellicott). The heart is established by God's undeserved approval (grace), not by keeping ceremonial food laws. "Those who have made these external observances the rule of their life have failed of the profit which they sought" (Ellicott). Guzik identifies the error as "a return to Mosaic ceremonies and laws that were fulfilled in Jesus."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 10 — "We have an altar from which those who serve at the tabernacle have no right to eat."

This is a key verse where traditions diverge:

**Protestant evangelical view:** Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic) states plainly: "Essentially, our altar is the cross — the centerpiece of the Christian gospel and understanding." Those who cling to the Levitical system have no right to this altar.

**Anglican view:** Ellicott takes a more nuanced approach. He explains that under the Law, priests ate portions of peace offerings and some sin offerings — but on the Day of Atonement, the high priest could not eat the sin offering (it was burned outside the camp). He then says: "For us there is but one sacrifice for sin, the efficacy of which endures for ever… we feed on Him who was slain for us, whose flesh was for the life of the world (John 6:51–56). We then (who are all 'priests unto God') 'have an altar of which,' on the very principles of their Law, 'they that serve the Tabernacle have no right to eat.'" He adds: "The stress is laid on the sacrifice, of which we eat, not upon the altar itself. If separately interpreted, the altar will be the place of sacrifice, the Cross." This Anglican reading leans toward a Eucharistic understanding ("we feed on Him") while still identifying the altar as the Cross.

**Catholic and Orthodox view:** (Not directly found in searches; noted here as a known reading.) The traditional Catholic interpretation sees "the altar" as the Eucharistic altar of the New Covenant, from which those still devoted to the old sacrificial system (unbelieving Jews) have no right to partake. This reading supports the sacrificial understanding of the Mass. The Orthodox tradition reads similarly, seeing the altar as the Holy Table where the Eucharist is celebrated.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 11 — "Although the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin, the bodies are burned outside the camp."

This refers to the Day of Atonement ritual (Lev 16:27). Ellicott notes that although the writer speaks of "the Holy Place," he probably has in mind the Holiest of All — the inner sanctuary — since the blood was taken within the veil only on the Day of Atonement. The key point: the priests received no portion of these sin offerings; the bodies were taken outside the camp and wholly consumed by fire. This sets up the typological parallel with Jesus in v. 12.

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1312-14

### v. 12 — "And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood."

Jesus fulfilled the Day of Atonement type: just as the sin offerings were taken outside the camp and burned, Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem's gate (Golgotha was outside the city — John 19:20). Precept Austin explains: "That 'outside' location symbolized rejection, removal of sin, and separation from uncleanness. The author now draws the stunning parallel: Jesus fulfilled that very pattern." The purpose was "that He might sanctify the people" — setting them apart from the profane and unto God, accomplished "through His own blood" (Precept Austin). Guzik adds: the suffering "outside the gate" was a symbol of His rejection by the Jews and the established religious system.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1312-14
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 13 — "Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore."

To "go to Him outside the camp" means identifying with the rejected Christ, even at the cost of being cast out of the religious community (Judaism, for the original readers). Guzik cites Spurgeon: "There is no being a Christian without being shut out of the world's camp." Ellicott writes: "Each one must for himself make choice either of the synagogue or of the church of Christ; between the two there can be no fellowship." "Bearing His reproach" means willingly sharing in the shame and rejection He experienced.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 14 — "For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come."

Ellicott sees two thoughts united: (1) we are free to leave the earthly city once held sacred (Jerusalem), for our hopes are not bound to any abiding earthly sanctuary; (2) we should not shrink from the reproach of Christ that severs us from kin, for by our very profession we are "strangers and sojourners" seeking the heavenly Jerusalem. He adds how impressive these words become "when read in the light of the events then unlooked for, yet so near at hand, issuing in the destruction of both Temple and city" (Jerusalem fell in AD 70). Guzik draws the practical application: for those who bear Christ's reproach, this world is the worst they will ever experience; for those who turn their back on Jesus, this life is the best they will ever have.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 15 — "Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name."

Because we have an altar (the cross) and a High Priest (Jesus), we offer sacrifices — but not bloody ones. Guzik identifies four essentials for proper praise: (1) it is offered "through Him" — on the grounds of Christ's righteousness; (2) it is "continually" — always, not occasionally; (3) it is a "sacrifice" — which may be costly or inconvenient; (4) it is "the fruit of lips" — spoken aloud, not merely internal thoughts. Precept Austin emphasizes the present tense: "let us continually offer up" calls for continuous, repeated, habitual action — "a lifestyle of worship." The phrase "fruit of lips" alludes to Hosea 14:2 (LXX), where the Hebrew reads "we will render our lips as bullocks" — i.e., as sacrifices (Ellicott). Spurgeon, cited by Guzik, says: "We are to utter the praises of God, and it is not sufficient to feel adoring emotions."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1315-16

### v. 16 — "And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased."

Praise is not the only sacrifice. "Do good" and "share" (freely impart to others — Ellicott) are also sacrifices pleasing to God. Precept Austin notes the structure: v. 15 has a vertical (God-directed) focus, while v. 16 has a horizontal (people-directed) focus. If the latter is lacking, the former is called into question (cf. 1 John 3:17; James 2:15–17). Guzik summarizes: "Praise and worship are important, but the Christian's obligation does not end there." Both the sacrifice of lips (v. 15) and the sacrifice of life in practical service (v. 16) please God.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1315-16

### v. 17 — "Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account. To this end, allow them to lead with joy and not with grief, for that would be of no advantage to you."

The section begins (v. 7) and ends (v. 17) with reference to church rulers. Verse 7 looked back to departed leaders; v. 17 addresses present leaders. Ellicott renders "submit yourselves" as "yield to them" — beyond obeying injunctions, be ready to comply with their wishes. The leaders "watch for your souls as having to give account" — an allusion to Ezekiel 3:18; 33:7; 34:10. Guzik cautions against abusing this: "A teacher should teach us to submit to God, not to himself" (Chuck Smith, cited in Guzik), referencing the abusive "Shepherding Movement." The warning is sober: if the flock causes their leaders to watch with grief (groaning), "this will both weaken their hands and bring on you the divine displeasure" (Ellicott). It is for the believers' own advantage ("profitable") that leaders serve with joy.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### vv. 18–19 — "Pray for us; we are convinced that we have a clear conscience and desire to live honorably in every way. And I especially urge you to pray that I may be restored to you soon."

The writer requests prayer, using the present imperative in Greek — implying they were already praying for him (Guzik). Ellicott notes the change to "I" in v. 19, suggesting "us" in v. 18 may include co-workers with the author, not the author alone. He also observes: the mention of a "good conscience" implies "some prejudice against the writer, or some mistrust of his motives, must have existed in the Church." But the warmth of v. 19 shows he knew himself to be beloved by most. The writer regarded their prayers as directly affecting whether and when he would be reunited with them (Guzik).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### vv. 20–21 — "Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with every good thing to do His will…"

Ellicott notes this is the only passage in Hebrews where the resurrection is mentioned apart from the ascension (elsewhere exaltation is contemplated as one act). The language draws from Isaiah 63:11 (LXX: "Where is he that raised up out of the sea the shepherd of the sheep?") and Zechariah 9:11 ("by the blood of thy covenant I have sent forth thy prisoners"). "In virtue of the blood of an eternal covenant God has raised up the Lord Jesus" (Ellicott). The covenant is "eternal" because Christ's blood ratified it once for all (Heb 9:15–18). The prayer is that God would "equip" (make complete, fully prepare) believers for every good thing to do His will, and that God Himself would work in them what is pleasing in His sight — through Jesus Christ. Guzik notes this is styled like the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:22–27. The doxology ("to whom be glory forever and ever") is directed to Jesus Christ, as in 2 Timothy 4:18 and Revelation 1:6 (Ellicott).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 22 — "I urge you, brothers, to bear with my word of exhortation, for I have only written to you briefly."

Ellicott renders: "Bear with the word of exhortation; for indeed it is in few words that I have written unto you." The whole Epistle is aptly called a "word of exhortation" (cf. Heb 5:11). Though it might be read aloud in under an hour, the writer considers it brief given the weighty subjects addressed. Precept Austin notes that "bear with" (*anechomai*) means "to tolerate patiently, to receive without resentment, and to accept even when difficult or weighty — which would have been especially true of the stern warning passages."

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_1322-25

### v. 23 — "Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you."

The Hebrew Christians knew of Timothy's imprisonment but had not heard of his release (Ellicott). This verse is one of the primary reasons some associate the letter with Paul — though the author does not identify himself. "If he come shortly" means sooner than the date at which the writer himself must depart (Ellicott). Guzik notes this shows the writer's personal connection to his readers and his intention to visit.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 24 — "Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send you greetings."

Ellicott explains that "They of Italy salute you" is consistent with two hypotheses: (1) the writer is in Italy and sends greetings from Italian Christians; or (2) the writer addresses a church in Italy and sends greetings from Italian Christians who are with him elsewhere. Guzik sees it simply as "Christians from Italy" who were with the writer, passing along their greetings. The greeting to "all your leaders and all the saints" reflects the dual structure already seen in vv. 7 and 17: leaders and the whole congregation.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hebrews/13.htm

### v. 25 — "Grace be with all of you."

A brief, standard apostolic benediction. Gill notes this is the writer's "usual benediction" — a simple closing that matches the epistolary form, placing the readers under God's grace as the final word of the letter.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-13/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hebrews/13.htm

## Denominational Differences and Other Views

### Areas where traditions notably differ:

**v. 4 — Marriage and celibacy:** As noted above, Gill (Baptist) explicitly criticizes "Papists" who deny marriage to clergy. The Catholic tradition reads this verse as affirming marriage's goodness for all while maintaining consecrated celibacy as a distinct calling. The Reformers universally rejected mandatory clerical celibacy, citing this verse among others.

**v. 10 — "We have an altar":** This is the most denominationally significant verse in the chapter. Evangelical Protestants (Guzik/Enduring Word) identify the altar straightforwardly as the cross. The Anglican Ellicott acknowledges a Eucharistic feeding ("we feed on Him who was slain for us") while still identifying the altar as the Cross. Catholic and Orthodox traditions have historically read "altar" as the Eucharistic altar of the New Covenant, supporting a sacrificial understanding of the Eucharist/Mass. (Direct Catholic/Orthodox commentary sources were not accessible in these searches.)

**v. 17 — Obedience to leaders:** All traditions affirm the duty of submission to spiritual leaders, but they differ on how far this extends. Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic) warns against the "Shepherding Movement" excesses — a caution particularly relevant in charismatic circles. More hierarchical traditions (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, some Lutheran) apply this to ordained clergy in apostolic succession. Congregational traditions see it as applying to local pastors/elders, with accountability ultimately resting with the congregation that recognizes them.
